title: Overseas acquisitions pay off for Hitachi logistics unit
cleaned_content: Japan’s Hitachi Transport System’s aggressive acquisitions in the United States and elsewhere have put it on track to almost achieve its medium-term global expansion plan, with overseas sales and profit escalating. Hitachi Transport System, the logistics arm of Japanese industrial conglomerate Hitachi, has strengthened its presence in the country’s transportation and logistics industry at a breakneck pace in recent years. Annual sales of Hitachi Transport System are now nearly 50 percent larger than those of Yusen Logistics, the logistics arm of Nippon Yusen Kabushiki Kaisha (NYK Line), Japan’s largest shipping firm by sales. Hitachi Transport System’s ambitious medium-term management plan, dubbed “Vision 2015,” calls for expanding annual sales and operating profit to 700 billion yen (US$5.7 billion) and 30 billion yen, respectively, in fiscal 2015, which started on April 1. Of the 700 billion yen sales target for the current fiscal year, 430 billion yen is to come from domestic operations and the remaining 270 billion yen from international operations. Hitachi Transport System has set the fiscal 2015 targets as a key step toward further growth in the global market with the ultimate goal of transforming itself into a major global player. Hitachi Transport System’s earnings results for fiscal 2014, which were released recently, show the company has made further progress toward achieving the fiscal 2015 targets. In fiscal 2014, the company’s sales rose 8.4 percent from a year earlier to 677 billion yen on a consolidated basis, while its group operating profit increased 1.0 percent year-over-year to 21 billion yen. Hitachi Transport System’s weak domestic performance was more than offset by its stellar international performance in the last fiscal year. Sales from domestic logistics operations rose 2.0 percent to 398 billion yen, while operating profit from domestic logistics operations shrank 9 percent to 26 billion yen. Sales from international logistics operations surged 20 percent to 258 billion yen, while operating profit from international logistics operations swelled a whopping 103 percent to 5.9 billion yen. Hitachi Transport System said that three overseas acquisitions made in the U.S., Hong Kong and Turkey in 2013 helped the company significantly boost its sales and operating profit from international logistics operations in fiscal 2014. In May 2013, Hitachi Transport System acquired a stake of about 87 percent in U.S. logistics firm James J. Boyle & Co. (JJB) as part of efforts to further expand its global operations. Hitachi Transport System also acquired a stake of about 85 percent in Hong Kong logistics firm CDS Freight Holding in July 2013 and purchased a 51 percent stake in Turkish logistics firm Mars Logistics Group in October 2013. Hitachi Transport System’s fiscal 2014 earnings results are based on Japanese accounting standards, but the company plans to fully switch to international accounting standards, called International Financial Reporting Standards, in fiscal 2015. For fiscal 2015, Hitachi Transport System expects 690 billion yen in sales under both Japanese and international accounting standards and operating profit of 25 billion yen under Japanese standards and 27 billion yen under international standards. Hitachi Transport System has operations around the world. In December 2012, the company became the first Japanese logistics services provider to make a full-scale foray into the Myanmar market by establishing a local subsidiary. As Myanmar emerges from many years of international isolation, it has drawn growing attention from foreign investors as the last economic frontier in Asia. Myanmar is rich in natural resources, has a relatively large population of about 51 million and is also sandwiched between China and India, the world’s two most populous countries. Myanmar has the potential to become a lucrative consumer market in the future if its economy develops smoothly and its people’s income grows. Thanks to its cheap labor, Myanmar has also attracted growing attention as an investment destination from Japanese and other foreign manufacturing companies that are reviewing their production and sourcing strategies in Asia amid rising labor costs in China.

title: After expanding in Europe, Asia, Dachser targets US growth
cleaned_content: Dachser, the German logistics provider, is poised to expand its relatively small share of the U.S. air and ocean freight business. With U.S. air and sea revenue already growing at double-digit rates, it plans to grow by leveraging its fully developed European network and its expansion in Asia, India and Latin America to provide more service to these markets for its U.S. customers. “We have invested heavily in completing our European network and taken a lot of new countries into our network worldwide, first of all in the Asia-Pacific region, but also the Americas, where we bought two Spanish companies that give us access to South America,” Dachser CEO Bernhard Simon said. “It also gives a lot of impetus to our North American business, which might also act as the hub for all of the Americas.” Dachser, which ranks as the eighth-largest global logistics provider, completed the acquisition last year of the other half of the joint venture in India with AFL Group that it didn’t already own. “That has given us a big impetus in the Asia-Pacific region because now we own all the companies there ourselves,” Simon said in an interview with JOC.com. Dachser generated revenue of 5.3 billion euros worldwide in 2014, an increase of 5.2 percent year-over-year. Although revenue from U.S. air-sea business is still a small share of its global business, it grew 16 percent to $192 million in 2014 on roughly the same increase in container volumes. Dachser anticipates growth of 15 to 18 percent in both revenue and volume in the U.S. trades in 2015. Dachser said it shipped almost 40,000 20-foot-equivalent units on U.S. ocean trade lanes last year. Dachser is building its U.S. business by focusing on the needs of small and medium-sized shippers. It has added contract logistics to its armory of products and operates a 202,000-square-foot warehouse in Tennessee for its automotive customers. Dachser has 220 employees in the U.S., mostly on the East Coast, but it is expanding in the Midwest, Phoenix, Seattle and San Francisco. It has targeted offices in 20 to 25 locations under its 2018 plan. “They are doing a great job of marketing in the U.S. and are becoming a much more recognizable brand,” said Dick Armstrong, chairman of Armstrong & Associates, a Wisconsin based logistics consultancy. He said the acquisition of 100 percent of its Indian subsidiary gives Dachser the opportunity to substantially increase its business in the subcontinent, where no single logistics provider dominates the market. The massive port congestion on the U.S. West Coast last year boosted Dachser’s U.S. business as a non-vessel-operating common carrier. “West Coast port congestion moved the shipping public more toward NVOCC solutions rather than carrier direct,” said Frank Guenzerodt, president and CEO of Dachser USA. “As an NVOCC, we were able to come up with different solutions and different routings to the East Coast.” The shippers that used Dachser to reroute their cargoes to the East Coast plan to maintain that routing, even though the International Longshore and Warehouse Union has ratified its new contract. “Although the East Coast rerouting is substantially more in transit time and cost, we have many clients who will continue to leave a certain percentage of their business on that routing just because who knows what will happen on the West Coast,” Guenzerodt said. Dachser saw about 15 percent of its total U.S. import volume shift from the West Coast to the East Coast, mostly to Charleston, Savannah and New York. It could have been more, but growth was limited by East Coast port congestion and available vessel space. As carriers withdraw from providing chassis at U.S. ports and cut back on inland deliveries, Guenzerodt sees an opportunity to increase market share. “The carriers are saying, ‘We don’t want to be involved in chassis, and we don’t want to be involved in tracking,’ so I think the opportunities for NVOs and freight forwarding are becoming bigger. Customers are not looking at a container to go from one port to another; they are looking for a container to go from supplier to consignee. An NVO and a freight forwarder can provide solutions that a carrier is not doing any more.” Although Dachser’s NVOCC business is growing, revenue has been hit by the decline in global freight rates during the last year, especially on the Asia-Europe trade lane, where they have dropped 75 percent. As an NVOCC in that trade, Dachser buys cargo space from carriers under three-month contracts, which it marks up and resells to its own customers at the prevailing spot rates. “Asia-Europe rates are down 75 percent, so it’s an unhappy situation for all of us,” said Thomas Reuter, Dachser COO for air and sea logistics. “It’s a constant battle trying to convince shippers that the rates should go up. They may have an advantage today, but who knows what tomorrow will bring.” In the trans-Pacific, Dachser buys space from carriers under annual contracts for resale to its customers. “The revenue is always affected by rate levels, which is a two-edged sword,” Guenzerodt said. “The decline in rates puts pressure on existing accounts because we have to follow up with the market reductions, but at the same time it gives us an opportunity to gain new customers who are shopping for savings in the market.”

title: Container Rates Continue to Experience Volatility, Especially on Shanghai Routes

Taking all routes into account, the WCI composite index went from $2,092 per 40-foot container in late February to $1,263/40ft in late April, before increasing again to $1,611 on 14 May. The reduction of spot rates is welcome by most shippers, but many non-contract shippers are not currently equipped to cope with huge volatility in their freight costs.” The World Container Index is the only weekly container pricing index based on actual agreed freight assessments reported by industry players in Asia, Europe and the U.S. and is not financed or backed by either shipper or carrier interests.

title: High-tech Manufacturing Execs Confident of Robust Growth
cleaned_content: The survey, conducted for UPS by IDC Manufacturing Insights, found that while high-tech companies still favor the strategy of off-shoring as a means to cut labor costs, a large number also have begun "right-shoring." This strategy optimizes the supply chain to take advantage of cost benefits and local resources to achieve the best customer service and overall profit margins. CITC also shows high-tech companies increasingly are entering emerging markets and exploring 3D printing for new product designs and prototypes. IDC polled 516 high-tech executives in North America, Europe, Asia Pacific and Latin America. Respondents were senior high-tech supply chain professionals. The results reveal an ongoing evolution in their supply chains that affects the placement of companies' owned facilities and the selection of their suppliers. "High-tech companies are building more flexibility into their shoring strategies and supply chains so they can respond better to demanding market dynamics," said Dave Roegge, high-tech marketing director at UPS. They're thinking more holistically about their strategies to evaluate their transportation costs and the time it takes companies to deliver goods. “Customer requirements change rapidly, especially considering the steady stream of high-tech innovations and the fact that there is little to no downtime between product generations,” Roegge said. Many of these companies see right-shoring as the solution. Right-shoring balances a number of factors to determine the proximity of sourced materials to production, warehousing and distribution. These metrics could include cost, quality and the time it takes to recover from any operational failures. Forty-five percent of survey respondents said they use right-shoring strategies. Offshoring, which moves manufacturing or assembly to countries with low labor costs, remains the most common strategy. Forty-seven percent of survey respondents said they offshore. Near-shoring, which moves manufacturing or assembly closer to the location of demand, continues to gain in popularity as companies improve service levels, reduce inventory in transit and seek greater control over product quality and intellectual property. Thirty-five percent of respondents said they near-shore. That’s a gain of 25 percentage points since 2010. “It’s about having a nimble supply chain,” Roegge said. Industry export growth continues; new opportunities emerge The growth outlook for high-tech exports is strong, the CITC survey showed. Forty-six percent of the respondents said they expect industry export growth globally to increase at the current pace over the next two years, while 28 percent of them expect faster growth. North American and Latin American respondents were the most optimistic about the future of high-tech exports. High-tech companies have successfully penetrated many emerging markets. Among survey respondents, 71 percent said they are already selling products in China, 45 percent in India and 42 percent in Brazil. Some high-tech markets once considered “emerging” have now emerged, but growth opportunities remain. The top three markets that high-tech companies are planning to enter this year are Brazil, Russia and India. Although new-market penetration is high, barriers to expansion continue to evolve. In 2013, the top barrier to expanding in emerging markets was difficulty assessing the likely appeal of products. In the most recent survey, 35 percent of survey respondents said navigating the regulatory environment was the new highest hurdle to expansion.

title: Lower Shipping Cost Trumps Desire for Quick Delivery, Study Says
cleaned_content: According to a survey of Canadian and U.S. shoppers conducted by Purolator International, the cost of shipping was identified most often as the single most important concern in terms of the delivery of their purchases. The survey found that 76 percent of Canadian consumers who made an online purchase from a U.S.-based retailer within the last six months, as well as 63 percent of U.S. online shoppers, identified shipping costs as very important; while 44 percent and 32 percent, respectively, said it was the single most important factor. Most shoppers chose extended delivery times for their online purchases; a majority of Canadians (78 percent) and Americans (58 percent) typically opted for shipping that took four days or longer. A majority of online shoppers in both countries (65 percent Canadian, 55 percent American) demonstrated this willingness to wait, responding that they have “very often” or “always” adjusted their delivery date to a longer period to obtain a reduced cost; and 37 percent and 28 percent, respectively, said the availability of an economical delivery option with a longer delivery time was very important to them. Two-thirds of shoppers in both nations identified a free shipping option as very important in their purchase decision making. “Even in this day and age of ‘I want it now,’ when consumers balance cost versus convenience, they most often fall on the side of cost,” said John Costanzo, president of Purolator International, the United States-based subsidiary of Purolator Inc., a provider of cross-border logistics between the U.S. and Canada. “These findings represent an opportunity for U.S. retailers looking to expand their reach across the northern border, by identifying what helps to drive – or hinder – final purchase decision making,” he added. An estimated $300bn of goods are imported into Canada from the United States annually, Costanzo noted. Shipping cost and time for delivery become especially of issue during the holiday shopping season, as 63 percent Canadians and 49 percent of Americans said they decided against purchasing a holiday item last year because of high shipping costs; 53 percent and 43 percent, respectively, decided against a holiday purchase because it would not be delivered in time. Postal Delivery Option and Cross-Border Concerns Regarding the delivery of their purchases, more than half (58 percent Canada, 57 percent U.S.) of the online shoppers ranked the reputation and reliability of the carrier as a very important consideration. In Canada, 80 percent of consumers surveyed said they would choose postal service delivery in order to obtain a lower shipping cost. A majority of Canadians (62 percent) and Americans (60 percent) said they see postal delivery as an acceptable alternative to other types of carrier delivery services. “Our postal hybrid solution, PuroPost, addresses this consumer preference, giving Canadians making online purchases from U.S. e-tailers a courier-like experience at a cost they are willing to pay,” Costanzo said. “With PuroPost, we can deliver to virtually all of the Canadian population with transit times that match industry standard ground trans-border services,” Costanzo added. Canadians purchasing from across the border are concerned about additional fees as well, with nearly half of those surveyed identifying taxes and tariffs as a very important concern – 15 percent of Canadians surveyed said it was the single most important factor in the decision for their purchase.

cleaned_content: West Coast dockside labor and management are certainly giving lip service to a renewed spirit of cooperation, following ratification of a new five-year contract, retroactive to July 1, 2014. Speaking for terminal operators, Pacific Maritime Association president and chief executive officer Jim McKenna said the pact "provides an important framework for the hard work ahead to overcome new competitive challenges and to continue to position the West Coast ports as destinations of choice for shippers worldwide." He insisted that "our interests are aligned" toward ensuring that the region's ports continue to operate efficiently, in order to handle future growth in container volumes. A statement by the International Longshore and Warehouse Union, whose members approved the contract by a margin of 82 percent, said it will “maintain excellent health benefits, improve wages, pensions and job safety protections; limit outsourcing of jobs and provide an improved system for resolving job disputes.” Los Angeles Mayor Eric Garcetti expressed gratitude over conclusion of the talks, thanking, among others, PMA and ILWU leadership “for their partnership in resolving their differences and putting this critical economic engine back on track.” Following tentative approval of the contract by ILWU and PMA negotiators in February of this year, longshore workers began clearing out the massive logjam of ships that were waiting to be unloaded at every major West Coast port. The backup was the direct result of a months-long slowdown by ILWU members, who, in protest of the drawn-out negotiations, and shielded by a lack of arbitration requirements, suddenly began withholding the labor that was needed to work the ships. Now the shipping channels are clear, and manning levels have returned to normal. But the pain that the union wrought hasn’t been forgotten. Importers and exporters had to incur huge expenses to get their products to market, or simply failed to do so. The Agriculture Transportation Coalition (AgTC) has estimated that losses in agricultural sales alone reached $1.75bn per month. Many of the hardest-hit companies were small or medium-sized businesses that operate in highly competitive markets, and can’t afford the slightest disruption to their supply chains. West Coast ports, so dominant in the age of trans-Pacific trade, lost a good deal of market share. Just in the month of April, East and Gulf Coast ports saw volume increases of 12 percent and 20 percent, respectively, while activity at West Coast ports dropped 4 percent, according to the Journal of Commerce. Much of that business will now return to the West Coast, of course, but shippers are paying serious attention to locating permanent alternative gateways. Retailers aren’t climbing aboard the Good Ship Harmony. The National Retail Federation issued a statement declaring itself “happy” to see the contract ratified. At the same time, NRF warned that “it’s not going to be long before we go through this process all over again.” The retailers’ group was even more blunt than that. “The past year was fraught with disruptions, slowdowns and partial shutdowns,” it said. “This is something we will no longer tolerate.” NRF called on negotiators to begin their talks early enough to have a new contract in place before the old one expires, “without active or passive threats to the economy and the millions of jobs dependent on our nation’s ports and supply chain. “The current process is impractical and unsustainable and fails to meet even the most basic requirements of a modern, global supply chain,” NRF said. Industry ought to go even further, to ask a basic question: should a highly compensated group of longshore workers be permitted to hold an entire nation’s economy hostage, when they don’t get their way? Congress just is beginning to tiptoe into the issue. Four Republican senators have introduced S. 1298, a bill that would monitor the impact of port disruptions on the economy, and set the stage for faster government intervention when they occur. The bill’s provisions sound fairly innocuous, calling for the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Bureau of Transportation Statistics to set up a port performance statistics program, and for the Secretary of Transportation to report to Congress on the state of port operations before and after the expiration of a longshore labor contract. The last thing we need is another statistics-stuffed government report that gathers dust on the shelf. But S. 1298, or a similar measure, is just the opening salvo in an effort to prevent a replay of the inexcusable events of the past year. Last time, all ILWU had to do was refuse to extend the arbitration provisions of the previous contract. Then its members could act with impunity, daring management to lock them out and take the blame for the shutdown. Employers didn’t bite, but the impact on the nation’s commerce was no less severe. AgTC has fired off a letter of support to the sponsors of S. 1298, calling it “a strong first step to demonstrating that Congress will not stand by idly and allow U.S. agriculture exports to lose our hard-earned foreign customers, due to port congestion and dysfunction relating to longshore labor negotiations (or any other factors).” Still to come is a means of measuring port productivity and determining the severity of a disruption – all the while preserving the union’s right to a fair wage and collective bargaining. For many whose livelihood depends on a smoothly functioning network of ports, however, the time for change is now.

title: Transportation Industry Drives Toward Non-Petroleum Energy
cleaned_content: In total, 8.5 percent of fuel used by the transportation sector came from non-petroleum sources in 2014. Biomass from corn-based ethanol - still supported by generous government subsidies - represented the largest non-petroleum energy source and was used primarily to fuel cars and other light vehicles. Use of natural gas to operate pipelines followed close behind. The report also shows smaller but still significant increases in the use of electricity, biodiesel and natural gas in vehicles. Climate change and fluctuating oil prices has made moving away from petroleum when possible a priority for governments and corporations alike. But it’s still uncertain which fuel will be the best and greenest replacement, according to Christopher R. Knittel, an MIT professor of energy economics. Ethanol, natural gas, hydrogen and electricity are all possibilities. "We don’t know where we’ll be 50 years from now," said Knittel. "There are four potential replacement for petroleum, and, ultimately, we don’t what's going to win out."

title: Allcargo Logistics joins Alibaba in e-commerce logistics

title: DCs Are Best Line of Defense for Driving Omnichannel Profits, Satisfying Customers
cleaned_content: But most retail stores are not set up to function as mini distribution centers (DCs). In fact, retailers will admit that while they are pulling off omnichannel processes in stores, they are not doing it profitably. The good news is that while many retailers feel that they are being slowly squeezed by Amazon, smart practices at their distribution centers can drive efficiencies, revenue and, more importantly, profits. The need to secure the sale at any cost has led to some extreme measures, with single items being expensively air-freighted from stores thousands of miles apart. For example, a colleague in Boston was looking for a new pair of winter hiking boots. After a record-breaking snowfall, he was unable to find a pair in his size within a 300-mile radius. Keen to satisfy the customer, the retailer sourced a pair – from Anchorage, Alaska – with free expedited shipping thrown in. That is a costly exercise to keep a customer happy, and cannot become the standard way of handling omnichannel fulfillment. It is equally costly to have out-of-stocks in the store or, worse, to be unclear what stock is being held. The latter can lead to problems such as "frozen inventory," where the retailer might think the store is holding the minimum acceptable level of stock for an item but due to theft, misplacement or poor stock-keeping practices the shelf is actually empty. It can take a long time, if ever, to spot and fix this kind of anomaly, and the out-of-stock could be fueling customer negativity over a long period. However, retailers do have strengths to draw on to help maintain stock visibility as well as their competitiveness. In particular, a well-run DC that correctly uses technology to accurately monitor inventory data can really make a difference. Retailers that have invested in RFID process automation at the DC and are source-tagging merchandise are ahead of the game. With an RFID solution integrated into warehouse management and inventory management systems of record, the creation of one hundred percent accurate advance shipping notices for retailers is possible. Every item ordered has its own unique identifier encoded into its label. The physical inventory contained in crates, pallets and individual boxes can be checked against the shipping manifest. In this manner, errors can be addressed before they are dispatched to the retailer, saving time for hard-pressed store staff to sort it out at their end. Automating shipment confirmation is key to making sure the truck loads are fully optimized in the right way. Real-time data means DC operations can be smarter with how they allocate, pick, pack and ship inventory to stores. Shipments based solely on historical retail data are not going to allow for flexibility or meet "real world" demand – the end result can be those high airfreight charges for single-item dispatch. Instead of sending a set number of shipments to stores at regular intervals based on last year's sales data, it is more profitable to supply what is actually selling today to outlets in different regions. RFID delivers a quick and accurate snapshot of specific local demand that the DC can go on to fulfill. This eliminates waste, reduces overall transportation costs and ensures that the right products are in the right place. To reduce transportation and handling costs, retailers want full trucks heading to stores – and full of things people are actually going to buy. Finally, the best practices found at the most optimized DCs can be migrated along the supply chain to flagship stores. Insightful retailers are beginning to look at RFID inventory management and RFID-enabled omnichannel fulfillment to turn flagship stores into mini-DCs to service smaller stores and the large surrounding populations. If such operations properly invest in their mini-DC status and do not just overload the existing staff with online fulfillment duties on top of regular store functions, then this can be a win-win strategy for retailers and customers. While online retailers may initially appear all-dominating, the use of innovative tools and strategies from source to shopper, combined with unmatched in-store personal service, gives aggressive brick-and-mortar retailers a competitive edge. And that ultimately results in increased customer satisfaction and profitability.

title: SEKO takes on Greenbriar as equity investor to speed growth
cleaned_content: With its management flexibility constrained by a fractured ownership structure, SEKO Logistics has brought in a private equity partner to recapitalize its balance sheet, transform its many local joint venture owners around the globe into shareholders and provide the resources to grow through acquisitions. Greenbriar Equity Group, which specializes in negotiated investments within the global transportation industry, took a substantial, but undisclosed stake in the Chicago-based logistics provider in May in a deal that allows SEKO to buy out local partners in many of its overseas affiliates, which are getting shares in the recapitalized company in place of their ownership in the local companies. “We can accelerate our growth by bringing in a partner like Greenbriar that has the expertise to analyze deals,” said SEKO CEO Bill Wascher. “In the next 24 months, you’re going to see SEKO making strategic acquisitions.” With Greenbriar as an equity partner, SEKO plans to acquire more logistics companies in overseas markets and also to buy trucking assets that will enable it to provide transport services for its customers. “As an asset-light organization, we may acquire last-mile providers in certain markets, mainly in the U.S.” Wascher said in an interview with JOC.com. “The (Greenbriar) private equity investment should help them become more recognizable and maybe more of a market force,” said Dick Armstrong, chairman of Armstrong & Associates, a logistics consultancy. “They have been around for some time now, but have never become a household word.” As a non-vessel-operating common carrier, SEKO saw its business increase sharply in 2014 when port congestion on the West Coast led many small and medium-sized beneficial cargo owners to seek alternate routing for their shipments, especially to the East Coast. “A lot of the BCOs don’t trust the steamship lines as much as they used to with regard to service and visibility, so more and more they are moving to NVOs,” Wascher said. “We are small time in relation to the whole ocean market, but our percentage growth is significantly higher than the market as a whole, because we are grabbing market share.” SEKO invested heavily to centralize its NVOCC business in 2013 after it saw its U.S. market share decline in 2012. In 2014 its global ocean freight volume jumped by more than 40 percent and by 38 percent in the U.S. “The recapitalization will give us added resources to grow even faster over the next five years,” said Jose Quesada, SEKO’s vice president of ocean services. “Our strong growth is due in part from centralization of the product, along with strategically moving away from being part of associations and not moving full container loads via co-loaders,” said Jose Quesada, SEKO’s vice president of ocean services. “Now we’re doing everything direct under our own NVOCC.” As an NVOCC SEKO ships about 100,000 twenty-foot-equivalent units annually. Imports through West Coast ports increased by 9 percent last year, and exports by 6 percent. East Coast shipments grew faster, with imports up 15 percent and export by 8 percent. Despite the settlement of the contract with the International Longshore and Warehouse Union this year, SEKO saw its volume of ocean freight imports moving through the East Coast through April 15 increase by 10 percent year-over-year, while West Coast imports increased by 6 percent. “More cargo is shifting to the East Coast because shippers are nervous about the West Coast,” Wascher said. “This year everybody thinks the West Coast is going to be a debacle again, because a number of owner operators went out of business and they are afraid the hours of service rules will affect the availability of trucks.” With its global ownership structure realigned through the Greenbriar investment, SEKO is already starting to replicate some of the supply-chain management services developed in the U.S. in overseas markets. For example, it is setting up a control tower in Ireland for its Medtech demo program, which manages the inventory of high-tech diagnostic equipment for medical-device manufacturers. “It will replicate in Europe that whole vertical market that we’ve had great success with in the U.S.,” Wascher said. SEKO is planning to replicate other supply chain management products and services in other global markets. Wascher was the leader of a team of executives who performed a management buyout of SEKO from U.S. Freightways in 2002. Since then, SEKO has increased its logistics business and revenues at double-digit rates, mainly in the U.S., the UK, Hong Kong and China. Those executives retain a “significant” stake in SEKO, but no longer have a controlling stake. One of the fastest areas of growth has come from selling technology it has developed for managing supply chains. The technology, called My SEKO Harmony, is an interface across a user’s supply chain that enables it to manage its purchase orders, its freight operating systems, warehouse systems and customs. “It gives them visibility from the front end of the supply chain all the way to the back end,” Wascher said. Looking ahead, Wascher is focusing its plans for growth on emerging markets. “Our trade in Europe and Asia is pretty well developed. We are expanding and developing our markets in Central and South America and the Caribbean. We intend to become a player in those markets, so we are starting with boots on the ground there and then start to market some of our vertical product there.”

title: Transport technology firms merge as shippers demand 'mobility'
cleaned_content: Increased demand for mobile, end-to-end networked computing systems in freight distribution is spurring acquisitions among transportation technology companies. For shippers, that increased merger activity should lead to greater innovation, hopefully driving even greater gains in supply chain efficiency. PeopleNet, a trucking technology company owned by $2.4 billion Trimble, last week purchased Cadec Global, a pioneer in fleet management technology and creator, in 1985, of the first automated truck driver’s log. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. Cadec joins a growing family of trucking and distribution technology companies owned by Trimble, including ALK Technologies, TMW Systems and GeoTrac. Trimble, which specializes in asset-locating or positioning technologies, acquired PeopleNet in 2011, TMW in 2012 and ALK in 2013. Since 1978, Trimble has acquired dozens of companies that offer, in some manner, navigation and positioning technology, from marine navigation to rail equipment management and construction and forestry logistics businesses. The technology needs of these disparate industries are converging as asset-tracking and management systems evolve to enable an interconnected “Internet of Things.” The fleet management technology industry will consolidate and become increasingly global, with the total number of onboard telematics units in vehicles in North and South America reaching 12 million by 2018, European technology research firm Berg Insight predicts. That will mean more data flowing from trucks and onboard devices back to motor carriers and fleet operators, with more data on freight being directed to shipper customers, as well. Increased use of onboard technology will also enable more vehicle-to-vehicle communications and interconnected supply chains. The Cadec acquisition gives PeopleNet, which offers Internet-based mobile computing and communications systems for trucking operators, new routes into the foodservice and shipper private fleet markets, Cadec’s target markets since its launch in 1976. Cadec customers include grocery chains such as Publix, Giant and Harris Teeter, food suppliers such as Land O’Lakes and Martin’s, restaurant chains such as Wendy’s and Braum’s and food distributors such as Saldino’s and Kuna Foodservice. The Manchester, New Hampshire-based company also has many fuel distribution customers. The merger comes at a critical point for shippers managing their own distribution fleets. As for-hire truck capacity gets tight and rates rise, shippers with private fleets are wringing as much efficiency and costs as they can from them. Foodservice companies are preparing for tough new regulatory requirements from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Combined, PeopleNet and Cadec Global can offer shippers a broader, integrated mobile computing network, Brian McLaughlin, PeopleNet president, said. “Cadec brings its expertise in world-class web enterprise, business intelligence and back-end analytics tools to the company, while PeopleNet brings its industry-leading mobile platforms, complementary M2M (machine-to-machine) and cloud-based technologies and infrastructure,” McLaughlin said in a statement. Under PeopleNet, Cadec Chief Customer Officer Angela Shue will become general manager of Cadec, working with the combined organization to develop new and innovative products for foodservice and private fleet customers. Other transportation technology companies offering mobility and asset-management services are growing by acquisition. Orbcomm, an asset-tracking company with its own network of low-earth-orbiting satellites, acquired competitor SkyWave in January. Omnitracs, a pioneer in trucking mobile communications, last year acquired XRS, and prior to that, Roadnet Technologies. Acquisition activity is likely to increase in the transportation technology market, as companies look to expand product portfolios they offer and build the scale they need to keep pace with growing customers.

title: Tanker Operators Tie Their Prosperity to Decreased Shale Oil Production, Boost in Oil Imports
cleaned_content: Tanker operators are pinning their hopes on a rise in U.S. crude oil imports as domestic shale oil extraction becomes increasingly unprofitable. Low oil prices have made crude extraction unprofitable for many U.S. producers, leading to a fall in U.S. rig counts and shrinking exploration and production investment. "Continued expansion of refinery capacity in Asia is likely to maintain growth in the global oil trade over the next five years," said Rajesh Verma, Drewry's tanker shipping lead analyst. "But demand from Asia alone will not be sufficient to sustain the improvement in tonnage utilisation. The only alternative source of growth is a recovery in U.S. oil imports, especially when declining European refinery capacity will mean lower import volumes to EU countries." Following two years of slow growth, the global trade in oil has accelerated over the past nine months due to increased stocking. And Drewry expects this trend to continue through to the end of 2016. However, thereafter we expect the influence of stocking activity to wane and hence continued development in trade will depend on rising Asian demand and a recovery in U.S. imports. On the supply side, tanker fleet growth is expected to remain muted in 2015, growing at just 1.3 percent year-on-year, before gathering momentum in 2016, when vessel deliveries are expected to rise over 60 percent compared to this year. Buoyant fleet growth will also be supported by a slowdown in scrapping activity. "Large vessels dominate the order book and this is a reflection of the expected increase in long voyage trades," said Verma. "And next year's opening of the widened Panama Canal will further support demand for the bigger classes of ships." Tanker vessel earnings are expected to remain strong on ample oil supply and the resultant softness in bunker prices.

title: On The Cutting Edge of Consumer Delivery
cleaned_content: The disruption of the retail segment by electronic commerce has forced merchandisers to focus on "last-mile" delivery. Traditional fulfillment systems were designed around the movement of large pallets from warehouses to supermarkets or big-box stores. With e-commerce, by contrast, customers shop online to purchase a single item that's shipped separately to the door. "It's never going to be profitable for a logistics company to deliver one parcel at a time for people who are not at home," says Moos. There's a big discussion going on about the need for same-day or even hour-specific delivery. But what customers really want, in Moos's view, is transparency. Certainty turns out to be more important than speed, even though so many e-commerce websites are pushing ever-faster delivery times. Another important element of a successful e-commerce offering is the presence of multiple delivery options. They've been shown to result in more finalizations of the shopping cart, says Moos. "You need to provide the options to people that suit their everyday lives the best," he adds. That might entail the ability to pick up parcels when they go to the supermarket. The idea is to place deliveries "in the normal, everyday life of the consumer." The locker box offers an alternative to expensive home delivery. It's currently enjoying popularity in Europe, especially in Denmark, Moos says. Unlike in a parcel shop, customers don't have to wait in line to pick up their packages. They go to a station, which can be in an existing store, type in a code and retrieve their items immediately. This so-called "click-and-collect" option offers merchandisers a big advantage, Moos says. And it helps traditional retailers to meld their operations with the growing world of e-commerce. title: UK to sell remainder of Royal Mail
cleaned_content: LONDON – The U.K.’s newly elected Conservative government today announced it will sell the state’s remaining 30 percent stake in Royal Mail to help reduce the country’s bulging deficit. The sale of the postal and delivery company, which is expected to raise up to 1.5 billion pounds ($2.3 billion), will start later this year, the Chancellor of the Exchequer George Osborne told Parliament. “There is no reason why we should hold a minority stake,” he said. The government sold an initial 60 percent stake in the 498 year old company via an initial public offering in October, 2013, that raised 3.3 billion pounds. The privatization drew criticism from opposition lawmakers and labour unions for selling the company too cheaply as the share price surged almost 90 percent following the IPO. The shares which were floated at 330 pence ($5) each closed at 526 pence on Wednesday. Royal Mail boosted operating profit in the year through March 29 by six percent to 740 million pounds on a one percent increase in revenue to 9.4 billion pounds. The company’s core domestic parcels business is facing stiff competition from Amazon, which launched its first same-day delivery service in the U.K. in October. GLS, the pan-European parcels unit, grew its operating profit to 115 million pounds from 108 million pounds on a six percent increase in delivery that boosted revenue by seven percent to 1.65 billion pounds.

title: CaroTrans launches new US-Japan export service
cleaned_content: CaroTrans is launching a new weekly less-than-container-load service between Southeastern U.S. and Japanese markets, cutting out transshipment and avoiding congestion at ports in Los Angeles and Busan. The New Jersey-based non-vessel operating common carrier said Wednesday the new service will take cargo from Atlanta, Georgia to a slew of major Japanese destinations including Tokyo, Yokohama, Kobe, Nagoya and Osaka. According to CaroTrans CEO Greg Howard, the new service is part of the carrier’s ongoing effort to employ new options for shippers, especially in the trans-Pacific lane. “Recent market challenges revealed the need for transportation alternatives for global supply chains,” Howard said in a statement. Congestion continues to haunt U.S. Pacific Coast ports, now months after the labor dispute between the International Longshore and Warehouse Union and port operators came to an end. “Today’s trans-Pacific supply chains require service flexibility and increased transportation choices to ensure reliable, timely freight delivery,” Howard said. “We’re committed to dependable, secure U.S.-Japan consolidation and deconsolidation and transportation services to ensure our clients are effectively serving their customers’ transpacific shipping needs.” CaroTrans will now offer 29-day freight service between Atlanta and Tokyo. Service between Atlanta and Yokohama will take 30 days. Service to Osaka, Nagoya and Kobe will each take 33 days. The new service will completely eliminate the need for transshipment and double handling at ports in Los Angeles and Busan. CaroTrans has promised that will translate fewer costs, speedier delivery, less risk and greater reliability and stability for cargo and cargo owner alike. To date, CaroTrans has added six new weekly, direct LCL and full-container-load services in the past six months. Last month, the NVOCC launched a weekly direct LCL service from Montreal to Le Havre, France, also pitched as an effort to cut costs and provide more options and flexibility to customers.

title: Empowered Consumers Change the Future of Retail, Survey Says
cleaned_content: Earlier this year 5,000 U.S. consumers were surveyed. The results indicate consumers plan to research and purchase more frequently using their mobile devices, they are influenced by social media, and free shipping continues to drive purchasing decisions. New in this year’s study, most consumers (93%) shop at small retailers: • 61 percent shopped at these locations because they offer unique products • 49 percent couldn't find what they needed from traditional stores • 40 percent wanted to support the small business community In addition, 40 percent of consumers have purchased from retailers based outside the U.S., with nearly half (49 percent) reporting they did so to find better prices, and 35 percent said they wanted items that couldn’t be found in U.S. stores. Online shoppers frequently change retail channels during their shopping experience. Better prices (57 percent) and selection (49 percent) are the top reasons for purchasing online after researching an item in-store. Nearly half (48 percent) of online shoppers have used ship-to-store in the past year, and 45 percent of those consumers made an additional purchase when picking up their online purchase. When a purchase is made online from a retailer that has an online and physical store, 39 percent of consumers who make returns prefer to ship the product back while 61 percent prefer to return the item to the store. When making an in-store return, 70 percent purchase an additional item compared to only 42 percent who make a new purchase while processing an online return. Respondents said they continue to use personal computers to shop and compare prices, and complement their use as they become more comfortable using mobile technology: 41 percent use their smartphone for research, while 30 percent make purchases. Online shoppers appreciate the convenience of smartphones on-the-go and in-store. Smartphone users project making more purchases on their device in the next year. Retailers need to continue to advance their mobile platforms, as 38 percent who have a mobile device but do not use it to make purchases said product images are not large or clear enough, and 30 percent said it's hard to compare products. Many consumers connect to shopping activities through social media with 43 percent reporting they discover new products on social media sites. Facebook is the most influential channel but shoppers also embrace visually-oriented sites such as Pinterest. Retail continues to evolve as some online shoppers consider using mobile technologies in store: 33 percent find electronic shelf labels appealing, 29 percent said they will consider mobile checkout, and 27 percent said they are open to using touch screens to receive information, make purchases or arrange deliveries. Free shipping remains the most important option during checkout according to 77 percent of online shoppers. More than half (60 percent) have added items to their cart to qualify for free shipping. The study provides insight to help retailers increase sales – 48 percent of online shoppers said they ship items to the store, with 45 percent of those saying they made additional purchases when picking up their orders. According to the report, only 62 percent of consumers are satisfied with the online returns process: 67 percent review a retailer's return policy before making a purchase, 66 percent want free return shipping, 58 percent want a hassle-free "no questions asked" return policy, and 47 percent want an easy-to-print return label. Compared to last year's study, more consumers are open to alternate delivery options. In 2014, 26 percent said they prefer to have packages delivered to locations other than their home, this year it rose to 33 percent. When not at home to sign for a package, 32 percent want it shipped to another convenient retail location. "The future of retail is driven by ever increasingly sophisticated and savvy shoppers who research at home and in a store, but more are turning to mobile as capabilities improve for online product display and promotion," said Alan Gershenhorn, UPS executive vice president and chief commercial officer. "They also want more flexibility and alternate delivery options."

title: Euro’s slide breathes new life into European 3PL sector
cleaned_content: Europe’s normally low-key logistics sector is suddenly hitting a high note, as a flurry of billion-dollar acquisitions kick-starts the long-stalled consolidation of a fragmented industry. U.S. companies are playing a key role in the makeover as they capitalize on the euro’s steep, yearlong slide against the dollar to snap up European logistics firms at attractive prices to expand their global networks. The U.S. presence will become more visible on European highways in the coming months, when Greenwich, Connecticut-based XPO Logistics paints its logo on the 7,700 trucks operated by France’s Norbert Dentressangle, its $3.5 billion acquisition. FedEx’s pending 4.4 billion-euro ($4.8 billion) acquisition of Dutch delivery company TNT Express will boost the Memphis-based giant’s share of the cross-border European express and parcels business from about 5 percent now to 17 percent, second only to Germany’s Deutsche Post DHL and ahead of U.S. rival UPS. XPO and FedEx cited the euro’s weakness against the greenback as a major impetus to their takeovers. Dentressangle, for example, would have been 20 percent more expensive a year ago. The slow but steady economic recovery in the troubled 19-nation eurozone also is playing a role in whetting U.S. companies’ appetite for trans-Atlantic expansion. “Europe has had a tough last few years,” XPO Logistics CEO Brad Jacobs said after tying up the Dentressangle deal. “My sense of the situation is that you’re seeing the beginnings of a rebound in the euro area.” Europe is the world’s largest contract logistics market, with more than a third of global revenue, although it’s likely to be overtaken by the Asia-Pacific region by 2017, according to logistics research and consulting firm Transport Intelligence. Europe, along with the U.S. and China, also will drive a 6.8 percent compound annual growth of global contract logistics through 2018, U.K.-based TI forecasts. “We believe that contract logistics growth will steadily accelerate in the coming years, although this relies heavily on European and U.S. economic performance improving and merely a gradual slowdown of the Chinese economy,” said David Buckby, a TI analyst. UPS’s decision to invest 1 billion euros to expand its European package delivery network underscores the region’s potential. “We will strongly expand our network in Germany and the rest of Europe,” said Frank Sportolari, UPS’s Germany chief. The Atlanta-based company “has lost time” since European regulators in 2013 shot down its own 5.2 billion-euro bid for TNT Express because of competition concerns, he told German business magazine Wirtschaftswoche. Asian companies seeking to expand their networks also could target European logistics interests, according to TI. Japanese companies, for example, are looking beyond their domestic market, pulling off a couple big-ticket deals this year — Japan Post’s $5.1 billion acquisition of Australia’s Toll Group and Kintetsu’s $1.2 billion takeover of APL Logistics — that could pave the way for others to flood into Europe to keep pace with the industry’s global consolidation. Additional moves in Europe by XPO can’t be ruled out either, with Jacobs saying the Dentressangle transaction that has catapulted it into the top 10 among global logistics providers is just the beginning. European companies themselves also have been active. Dentressangle paid $750 million for Jacobson, a Des Moines, Iowa-based contract logistics company last September, sparking XPO’s interest in the privately held French company. Denmark’s DSV was involved in discussions in December about the acquisition of California-based UTi Worldwide in what would have been its biggest takeover since it paid 750 million euros for Belgium’s ABX Logistics in 2008. That the deal collapsed hasn’t dulled DSV’s growth ambitions. “We have a clear intention of further expanding our network through additional acquisitions, provided we can find the right candidates,” CEO Jens Bjorn Andersen said. “We are keeping an eye out for companies that can strengthen DSV’s network outside Europe, in particular.” Panalpina CEO Peter Ulber said the Swiss forwarding and logistics giant would be ready to participate in the consolidation process by the end of 2016, after it rolls out a new IT and management system across its global network. Denmark’s DFDS, northern Europe’s largest short-sea and logistics company, is also on the prowl after a 56 percent jump in pretax profit in 2014. “Based on our solid performance, we are well-positioned to expand our activities through both organic growth and acquisitions, should the right opportunities materi-alize,” CEO Niels Smedegaard said. DFDS hasn’t pulled off a big-ticket deal since its $425 million acquisition of Maersk’s Norfolkline subsidiary in 2011, and, having pulled out of bids for European roll-on, roll-off shipping operator Scandlines, Turkey’s UN RO-RO and Sea France, it might opt to beef up its logistics business. Dascher, the $5.3 billion-a-year German logistics provider, also is on the takeover trail, eyeing acquisitions across the Atlantic to expand its relatively small share of the U.S. ocean and air freight markets. Despite the recent run of deals, the transportation and logistics sector trails other industries in M&A activity and consolidation. There were 195 transactions worth a combined $13.8 billion in 2014, down from 248 deals worth $29.9 billion in 2013, according to financial services firm Dealogic. Even as their domestic markets rally, European logistics companies are bracing for tough times beyond their shores. The global transportation and logistics markets are under extreme pressure, according to Rudiger Grube, CEO of Deutsche Bahn, Germany’s giant state railway and a major logistics player through DB Schenker, its 15 billion euro-a-year subsidiary. These pressures are taking their toll on some of Europe’s largest companies, none more so than Damco, Maersk’s Group’s troubled logistics business that continues to lose market share as it struggles to climb out of the red. Although Damco managed to trim its first- quarter 2015 loss to $9 million from $10 million a year earlier, revenue declined by $66 million to $749 million, ocean traffic dipped 2 percent and air freight crashed by 19 percent. The company is Maersk’s worst-performing business, with the rate of return on invested capital deteriorating to a negative-11.2 percent in the first quarter from 9.3 percent a year earlier, while the group’s overall figure improved to 13.8 percent from 10 percent. Analysts see Damco as a potential disposal when it emerges from intensive care. Deutsche Post DHL, the world’s biggest logistics company, also is struggling to turn around its floundering forwarding unit, whose botched transformation program it blamed for the group’s reduced first-quarter profit and abandoning its original 2015 earnings forecast last year. The company suspended a pilot program to implement new IT systems before they were rolled out across its global network because it was hurting day-to-day operations. “We will take time out to see if we can reduce the complexities before we decide on a new rollout,” Chief Financial Officer Larry Rosen said. Industry analysts also are charting the progress of another major operator, CEVA Logistics, two years after the Netherlands-based company won support from bondholders for a debt-for-equity swap that slashed net debt by 1.2 billion euros. The company, owned by U.S. private equity group Apollo Global Management, launched a new business model in 2015 that eliminated the previous region-based structure in favor of 17 local geographic clusters of countries with uniform governance standards and business rules. “We are seeing the visible impact of the operational improvements, ongoing streamlining of processes and greater responsiveness to our customers’ needs enabled by the new operating model,” CEO Xavier Urbain said when he unveiled an 18.6 percent increase in adjusted first-quarter earnings to $51 million as ocean freight volume rose 5 percent, air cargo traffic increased 5.2 percent and freight management revenue grew 6.1 percent. While small and medium-sized companies struggle to survive amid fierce competition, bulging overcapacity and rising investment demands — the number of insolvencies in the U.K. logistics sector soared 20 percent year-over-year in 2014 to 221, double the 2010 figure — the largest companies are boosting their markets at home and abroad. Deutsche Post’s DHL Express unit again dominated the group’s early 2015 performance, with first-quarter operating profit surging 20 percent to 332 million euros, outpacing a 12.5 percent growth in revenue to 3.2 billion euros. The company plans to create as many as 10,000 jobs by 2020 in Germany alone as it races to keep up with the explosive growth in e-commerce. “We want to be the global market leader in logistics for e-commerce,” CEO Frank Appel told shareholders at the annual general meeting at the end of May. To achieve this, the group plans to expand DHL’s domestic parcel business model across its global network. Swiss giants Kuehne + Nagel and Panalpina are leveraging their market-leading ocean and air freight market shares to expand their contract logistics operations against the backdrop of a surging Swiss franc that undermines their bottom lines while strengthening their ability to expand their networks and mount acquisitions. Kuehne + Nagel’s net earnings stalled in the first quarter following a record 1 billion-franc ($1 billion) profit in 2014 as the currency soared following the Swiss central bank’s January decision to stop intervening to cap its value against the euro. Panalpina more than doubled its operating profit to 116.7 million francs in 2014, with contract logistics losses tumbling to 8.2 million francs from 49.9 million in 2013, helped by the disposal of money-losing facilities and unprofitable trucking operations. The logistics business swung to a 1.2 million-franc profit in the first quarter of 2015 from a year-earlier loss of 5.5 million francs as it exited from underperforming sites. Europe’s state-owned logistics giants are finding it tougher to increase profits as nimbler private companies eat into their markets. DB Schenker’s adjusted earnings stalled at 332 million euros in 2014, but contract logistics stood out as a star performer, with revenue surging more than 10 percent to 2 billion euros, while air and ocean volumes posted modest growth and rail freight declined. France’s SNCF Logistics boosted its profit to 431 million euros in 2014 from 337 million in 2013 on revenue that was flat at 8.8 billion euros. The parent of Geodis relied on its operations beyond Europe, which grew 5.8 percent and offset a 0.2 percent decline in its domestic market. Leaner medium-sized private companies that have built up a solid customer base in key markets are outperforming the state-owned behemoths. Dascher boosted 2014 revenue by 5.2 percent to 5.3 billion euros as it capitalized on the trend toward outsourcing internationally complex logistics to drive organic growth. Dascher also expects integrated supply chain solutions for multinational customers to be a major source of growth in the future. “Our global network, enhanced by our customized contract logistics solutions in Europe, Asia and the U.S., as well as our own air and sea freight network, allow us to create complete supply chains,” said Bernhard Simon, CEO of the family owned company. This optimistic outlook is gaining traction across Europe’s logistics sector as a cheap euro boosts exports of increasingly competitive European products worldwide and a recovering continental economy improves prospects in domestic markets.

title: Forwarder Lynden International acquires US-based Haas Industries
cleaned_content: Freight forwarder Lynden International acquired Haas Industries, strengthening Lynden’s home delivery, trade show and specialized delivery services in the U.S. and Canada. The combined organizations, which merged June 1, have 26 company-owned service centers throughout the U.S. and Canada, including locations in Alaska, Hawaii and Puerto Rico. The merger of Haas into Seattle-based Lynden International “will allow us to provide a wider array of services with greater reach,” the companies said in a statement. "The combination of our two companies will allow us to continue building our domestic service portfolio,” John Kaloper, vice president of Lynden’s America Division, said. The rise of e-commerce is spurring interest in home delivery and specialized delivery capabilities, such as delivering and installing appliances or equipment at homes or businesses. Transportation providers of various types, from less-than-truckload carriers to third-party logistics companies, are either adding or acquiring home delivery operations. Lynden International is the freight forwarding arm of the multimodal Lynden family of companies, which offer global air and ocean forwarding, logistics, trucking and Alaska shipping services. Lynden pioneered freight delivery to Alaska via the Alaska Highway in the 1950s. In addition to trucking, the company is involved in barge, air cargo and intermodal rail shipping. The forwarding operation recently expanded in Eastern Canada, opening a service center in St. John’s, Newfoundland, in part to support the province’s growing oil and gas industry. Haas, based in Haymarket, California, was founded in 1989. The company now operates as Lynden International. The companies did not disclose financial terms of the acquisition.

title: The Age of 'Click-and-Collect' Lockers for Home Delivery
cleaned_content: The notion of "click and collect" allows customers to order product in any way they wish, then pick up the goods at the location of their choice – whether the store, their homes or a locker. It can apply to a broad variety of products, from fast food to home-improvement items. The idea of the locker is the latest addition to the growing menu of e-commerce delivery options. It can be located outside of a store, within a retail outlet, at a railway station, in a parking lot or even within a multi-tenant apartment building. Or it can be placed at the location of a special event. Traditional store pickup often entails waiting in long lines at a service counter. Lockers placed up front, by contrast, allow for instant access to goods by the buyer. In such instances, lockers “automate the process, and make it quick and convenient,” Savage says. He views the locker option as an idea whose time has come. The reason, he says, is the arrival of technology that enables real-time communication with back-end systems. At the same time, consumer expectations of service are developing rapidly, to the point where ease of delivery becomes a key selling point for the retailer. Lockers can benefit the retailer as well, in that they can draw on merchandise that’s already on hand. In effect, the store becomes a distribution center for the fulfillment of online orders. Still, “the retailer must be able to make a promise to the customer, and keep that promise,” Savage says. “That takes a holistic approach.” At the moment, the concept of lockers is more popular in Europe. But Savage believes it will quickly migrate to the U.S. “Interest level is at an all-time high,” he says. “In the next 12 to 18 months, this explodes.” To view the video in its entirety, click here

title: Post-acquisition, XPO looking beyond Norbert Dentressangle
cleaned_content: Now that he’s closed his biggest acquisition yet — European logistics operator Norbert Dentressangle SA — Bradley S. Jacobs is already looking for new prospective purchases as he transforms U.S.-based XPO Logistics into a “global supply chain solutions provider.” XPO Logistics on June 8 finalized the purchase of all shares of Norbert Dentressangle held by the Dentressangle family, representing 67 percent of the Lyons, France-based company’s stock. Norbert Dentressangle iconic red trucks — the company is one of the largest truck operators in Europe — are already being refitted with XPO signage. XPO’s first European trucks will be rolled out during the Tour de France bicycle race, debutting at the Grand Départ of the race July 4. XPO’s odyssey from a $150 million company in 2011 to one with an $8.5 billion 12-month revenue run rate today has more twists and turns than the Tour de France course. Jacobs and his team have built XPO rapidly through more than a dozen acquisitions, from freight brokerage firms to last-mile logistics and intermodal drayage companies. “We believe scale is imperative in this business to serve customers effectively.” Jacobs said in an interview in April. Norbert Dentressangle gives XPO significant global reach and scale beyond North America and beyond Europe as well, with access to Asia-Europe trade lanes. The acquisition is expected to increase XPO's global freight forwarding revenue to approximately $425 million a year. In 2014, Norbert Dentressangle was a $5.5 billion company, with offices in 25 countries and 42,600 employees. In 2014, XPO reported $2.4 billion in revenue. XPO now claims to be the second-largest freight brokerage, after C.H. Robinson Worldwide, the largest provider of last-mile logistics for heavy goods and the largest manager of expedited shipments. Combined, XPO and Norbert Dentressangle would have ranked 12th on the JOC.com/SJ Consulting Group list of Top 50 Global 3PLs ranked by revenue in 2014. XPO is looking at more European acquisitions, as well as North American companies. “We are actively looking at other great companies to buy in Europe that would fit in well with the footprint that we just established,” Jacobs told JOC.com in May. “Europe has had a tough last few years. My sense of the situation is that you’re seeing the beginnings of a rebound in the euro area.” The company is actively seeking to expand its operations in last-mile, intermodal, global forwarding, supply chain, expedite and freight brokerage services. Now that XPO has evolved into global company, Jacobs said he feels less limited by geography. Norbert Dentressangle was looking at several acquisitions in Europe, “and they look pretty good to us too.”

title: The 'Uberfication' of Home Delivery
cleaned_content: "People are tired of not knowing when something is coming to them," says Sion. Yet he believes the problem will disappear within two to three years. The reason is the extension of the personal-transportation option, pioneered by Uber for passengers, to packages. An Uber-like model will give customers transparency as to when their packages will arrive. Sion believes the market is dictating its development. "People are more and more expecting same-day and one-hour service," he says. "And they expect to be part of the experience." An urban setting, because of its high concentration of population, is likely the best place to develop the service. But even in less-crowded areas, it could provide customers with complete driver visibility and delivery within a matter of hours, Sion says. He believes this service-intensive approach will become essential to the survival of retailers, much as the creation of the internet eventually dictated that every company would have a website. "The concept is changing the experience for the customer," he says. Sion isn't sure whether an enhanced delivery offering like that of Bringg would compete with Amazon, Google and other established players, or work with them. "Amazon is a possible customer," he says, "but it’s not our target." Regardless of who is offering it, an on-demand service platform "equates with customer retention," Sion says. title: U.S. Manufacturing Fuels Shipping on St. Lawrence Seaway
cleaned_content: According to the St. Lawrence Seaway, shipments of steel, aluminum, wind turbines and other heavy machinery were up by 5 percent to 629,000 metric tons from April 2 to May 31. Steel and Canadian aluminum headed to U.S. Great Lakes ports such as Oswego, Detroit and Toledo to be used in the thriving automotive industry. Local manufacturers also exported mining equipment via the Port of Milwaukee to Europe. Looking ahead, U.S. energy projects are expected to boost wind turbine shipments in the Great Lakes this season. The Port of Duluth-Superior has already booked 20 ships for its general cargo dock this year, including multiple loads of wind turbine components. The Port Authority recently broke ground on its $17.7m Port of Duluth Intermodal Project to enhance its heavy-lift and project cargo capacity. While it was another late start to the season due to icebreaking constraints, grain from Canada and the U.S. continued to flow out of the St. Lawrence Seaway to export markets, totaling 1.9 million metric tons so far this season, up 7 percent over 2014. And dry bulk shipments, including road salt, coke for steel production, and construction materials totaled 1.7 million metric tons, up four percent. Despite these star performers, year-to-date total cargo shipments via the St. Lawrence Seaway were 6.4 million metric tons, down by 7 percent compared to 2014 due to low global prices for North American iron ore and coal exports. Iron ore shipments via the Seaway were down 30 percent, while coal shipments dipped 27.5 percent compared to the same period the year before.
